{{Short description|AI standards for robustness and data privacy}}
{{Artificial intelligence}}
'''Trustworthy AI''' refers to [[artificial intelligence]] systems that are designed to have transparent reasoning, are [[Explainable artificial intelligence|explainable]] (XAI), accountable, robust, fair and honest, respectful of data privacy, and [[AI alignment|steerable or alignable with human goals]].<ref>[https://www.aepd.es/sites/default/files/2019-12/ai-ethics-guidelines.pdf Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI], The Independent High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence, set up by the European Union, April 8, 2019 (Spanish Government website)</ref><ref name="fairness">{{Cite journal |last1=Mehrabi |first1=Ninareh |last2=Morstatter |first2=Fred |last3=Saxena |first3=Nripsuta |last4=Lerman |first4=Kristina |last5=Galstyan |first5=Aram |date=13 July 2021 |title=A Survey on Bias and Fairness in Machine Learning |url=https://doi.org/10.1145/3457607 |journal=ACM Computing Surveys |volume=54 |issue=6 |pages=115:1–115:35 |doi=10.1145/3457607 |arxiv=1908.09635 |s2cid=201666566 |issn=0360-0300}}</ref><ref name="aima4">
{{Cite book | last1=Russell | first1 = Stuart J.| last2=Norvig | first2 = Peter| year = 2021| url=https://www.pearson.com/us/higher-education/program/Russell-Artificial-Intelligence-A-Modern-Approach-4th-Edition/PGM1263338.html | title=Artificial intelligence: A modern approach| publisher=Pearson |isbn=9780134610993 |edition=4th | pages=5, 1003  | access-date=September 12, 2022 }}</ref><ref>[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LUn8IjZKBPg&pp=0gcJCfwAo7VqN5tD How to Govern AI — Even If It’s Hard to Predict], Helen Toner, [[TED (conference)|TED]]</ref>

== Terminology ==
Recent work in [[AI ethics]] distinguishes trustworthiness and trustability as two different conditions relevant to trustworthy AI. Trustworthiness is concerned with whether an AI system or the institutions deploying it merit trust by being reliable, fair, and accountable. Trustability, on the other hand, is the prior question of whether a given entity is even the kind of thing to which interpersonal trust can coherently apply as opposed to mere instrumental reliance.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Jannel |first=Romaric |last2=Tallant |first2=Jonathan |date=2026 |title=Trustability and trustworthiness: conceptual foundations and the case of AI |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43681-025-00839-w#citeas |journal=AI and Ethics |publisher=Springer |volume=6 |issue=13 |doi=10.1007/s13347-025-00982-6|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Transparency in AI involves making the processes and decisions of such systems understandable to users and stakeholders. Accountability means that protocols for addressing adverse outcomes or [[algorithmic bias]]es that may arise include designated responsibilities for oversight and remediation. Robustness and security attempt to ensure that AI systems perform reliably under various conditions and are safeguarded against malicious attacks.<ref>{{Cite web |title='Trustworthy AI' is a framework to help manage unique risk |url=https://www.technologyreview.com/2020/03/25/950291/trustworthy-ai-is-a-framework-to-help-manage-unique-risk/ |access-date=2024-06-01 |website=MIT Technology Review |language=en}}</ref>

Harmlessness can be achieved by refusal training: training the models to avoid problematic requests, and by adding filters to detect and prevent discussion on biased, unethical, or dangerous outputs.<ref name="fairness" />

In the field of machine learning research, there have been many similar studies carried out under the notion of '''trustworthy machine learning'''.<ref>Varshney, Kush R. (2022). ''Trustworthy Machine Learning: Concepts for Developing Accurate, Fair, Robust, Explainable, Transparent, Inclusive, Empowering, and Beneficial Machine Learning Systems''. Chappaqua, NY: Independently published. {{ISBN|979-8411903959}}.</ref><ref>Varshney, Kush R. (2019). "Trustworthy Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence". ''XRDS: Crossroads, The ACM Magazine for Students''. '''25''' (3): 26–29. {{doi|10.1145/3313109}}.</ref> The annual conference known as the IEEE Conference on Secure and Trustworthy Machine Learning (SaTML), organized by the IEEE Computer Society Technical Committee on Security and Privacy, has also been held since 2023.<ref>{{cite web |title=IEEE Conference on Secure and Trustworthy Machine Learning |url=https://satml.org/ |access-date=20 August 2026}}</ref>

== Techniques and ITU standardization ==
Trustworthy AI creation is a goal of AI governance and policymaking. To achieve transparency and data privacy, several [[privacy-enhancing technologies]] (PETs) can be used. These include:<ref>{{Cite web |title=Advancing Trustworthy AI - US Government |url=https://www.ai.gov/strategic-pillars/advancing-trustworthy-ai/ |access-date=2022-10-24 |website=National Artificial Intelligence Initiative |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=TrustworthyAI |url=https://www.itu.int:443/en/ITU-T/Workshops-and-Seminars/2022/0901/Pages/TrustworthyAI.aspx |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221024211101/https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-T/Workshops-and-Seminars/2022/0901/Pages/TrustworthyAI.aspx |archive-date=2022-10-24 |access-date=2022-10-24 |website=ITU |language=en-US}}<br />{{Creative Commons text attribution notice|cc=by4|from this source=yes|author=the [[International Telecommunication Union]]|url=https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-T/Workshops-and-Seminars/2022/0901/Pages/TrustworthyAI.aspx}}</ref>
* [[Homomorphic encryption]] for computing with encrypted data without ever decrypting it.
* [[Federated learning]] and [[secure multi-party computation]] (MPC) for distributing the model training without sharing information between the learning centers and computing servers.
* [[Differential privacy]] for exposing statistical data while guaranteeing that no private information is exposed.
* [[Zero-knowledge proof]] - providing proven validity for statements without disclosing any extra information.
A work programme for achieving Trustworthy AI was set up by the [[International Telecommunication Union]] (ITU), an agency of the [[United Nations]], initiated under its [[ITU AI for Good|AI for Good]] programme.<ref name=":0" /> Its origin lies with the [[ITU-WHO Focus Group on Artificial Intelligence for Health]], where a strong need for both privacy and analytics created demand for a standard in these technologies.

In 2020, AI for Good moved online, and the TrustworthyAI seminar series was established to initiate discussions on these topics. This eventually led to standardization activities.<ref>{{Cite web |title=TrustworthyAI Seminar Series |url=https://aiforgood.itu.int/about-ai-for-good/discovery/ |access-date=2022-10-24 |website=AI for Good |language=en-US}}</ref>

In the [[European Union]], the Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI say that trustworthy AI should be lawful, ethical, and robust. In practice, the guidelines define seven requirements for trustworthy AI: human agency and oversight; technical robustness and safety; privacy and data governance; transparency; diversity, non-discrimination and fairness; societal and environmental well-being; and accountability.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ethics guidelines for trustworthy AI |url=https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/ethics-guidelines-trustworthy-ai |access-date=2026-06-06 |website=digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu |language=en}}</ref>

=== Multi-party computation ===
[[Secure multi-party computation]] (MPC) is being standardized under "Question 5" (the incubator) of [[ITU-T Study Group 17]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Shulman |first1=R. |last2=Greene |first2=R. |last3=Glynne |first3=P. |date=2006-03-21 |title=Does implementation of a computerised, decision-supported intensive insulin protocol achieve tight glycaemic control? A prospective observational study |journal=Critical Care |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=P256 |doi=10.1186/cc4603 |issn=1364-8535 |pmc=4092631 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Homomorphic encryption ===
[[Homomorphic encryption]] allows for computing on encrypted data, where the outcomes or result is still encrypted and unknown to those performing the computation, but can be deciphered by the original encryptor. It is often developed with the goal of enabling use in jurisdictions different from the data creation (under, for instance, [[GDPR]]).{{Citation needed|date=June 2024}}

ITU has been collaborating since the early stage of the ''HomomorphicEncryption.org'' standardization meetings, which has developed a standard on homomorphic encryption. The fifth homomorphic encryption meeting was hosted at [[World Triathlon Aquathlon Championships|ITU HQ]] in [[Geneva]].{{Citation needed|date=June 2024}}

=== Federated learning ===
Zero-sum masks as used by [[federated learning]] for privacy preservation are used extensively in the multimedia standards of [[ITU-T Study Group 16]] ([[VCEG]]) such as [[JPEG]], [[MP3]], [[H.264]], and [[H.265]] (commonly known as [[MPEG]]).{{Citation needed|date=June 2024}}

=== Zero-knowledge proof ===
Previous pre-standardization work on the topic of [[zero-knowledge proof]] has been conducted in the ITU-T Focus Group on Digital Ledger Technologies.{{Citation needed|date=June 2024}}

=== Differential privacy ===
The application of [[differential privacy]] in the preservation of privacy was examined at several of the "Day 0" machine learning workshops at AI for Good Global Summits.{{Citation needed|date=June 2024}}

== Mozilla "Rebel Alliance" ==
In January 2026, the [[Mozilla Foundation]] and its subsidiaries announced a strategic shift to deploy their entire $1.4 billion reserve into building what foundation president [[Mark Surman]] termed a "rebel alliance" for trustworthy AI.<ref name="CNBC_Surman">{{cite news |last=Capoot |first=Ashley |title=Mozilla building an AI rebel alliance to take on OpenAI, Anthropic |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2026/01/27/mozilla-building-an-ai-rebel-alliance-to-take-on-openai-anthropic-.html |publisher=[[CNBC]] |date=2026-01-27 |access-date=2026-01-27}}</ref> Framed by Surman as a mission-driven alternative to the market dominance of [[OpenAI]] and [[Anthropic]], the initiative seeks to establish an [[open-source software|open-source]] AI stack by 2028.<ref name="CNBC_Surman" /><ref name="PYMNTS_Mozilla">{{cite news |title=Mozilla Recruits Partners to Take on AI Goliaths |url=https://www.pymnts.com/artificial-intelligence-2/2026/mozilla-recruits-partners-to-take-on-ai-goliaths/ |publisher=PYMNTS |date=2026-01-27 |access-date=2026-01-27}}</ref>

The alliance includes several startups funded via Mozilla Ventures, specifically focusing on decentralized governance and transparency:<ref name="WebProNews_Mozilla">{{cite news |title=Mozilla's Rebel Alliance Wages Open AI War on OpenAI, Anthropic |url=https://www.webpronews.com/mozillas-rebel-alliance-wages-open-ai-war-on-openai-anthropic/ |publisher=WebProNews |first=Elizabeth| last=Morrison|date=2026-01-27 |access-date=2026-01-27}}</ref>
* Trail: A firm developing AI compliance frameworks for regulated industries.
* Transformer Lab: A developer of open-source tools for AI model management.
* Oumi: A platform for training and deploying open-source models.

The "rebel alliance" terminology is a historical reference to Mozilla's efforts in 1998 to challenge Microsoft's [[browser wars|browser monopoly]].<ref name="CNBC_Surman" /> While the $1.4 billion in funding is significant, it has been contrasted with the tens of billions in capital raised by proprietary competitors like OpenAI.<ref name="PYMNTS_Mozilla" /><ref name="WebProNews_Mozilla" />

== Debate ==
Some philosophers argue that current AI systems are best understood as tools that are not genuine targets of interpersonal trust. They argue that trust should be directed toward the human and institutional arrangements that govern the systems' design, deployment, and oversight. This stance supports interpreting "trustworthy AI" as trustworthy governance and use of AI rather than trust in the artifacts themselves.<ref name=":1" />

According to Zanotti et al., a common argument is that "An entity X is trustworthy only if X has the right motivations, goodwill and/or adheres to moral obligations towards the trustor" and that AI systems lack these characteristics. Zanotti et al. reject this conclusion, arguing that a definition of trustworthiness for AI systems doesn't have to mirror the definition for humans and could instead be based on reliability coupled with value-laden features, such as fairness, transparency, and respect for human autonomy.<ref name=":02">{{Cite journal |last1=Zanotti |first1=Giacomo |last2=Petrolo |first2=Mattia |last3=Chiffi |first3=Daniele |last4=Schiaffonati |first4=Viola |date=2024 |title=Keep trusting! A plea for the notion of Trustworthy AI |journal=AI & Society |language=en |volume=39 |issue=6 |pages=2691–2702 |doi=10.1007/s00146-023-01789-9 |hdl=11311/1252561 |issn=0951-5666 |doi-access=free |hdl-access=free}}</ref>

[[Stuart J. Russell]] and [[Peter Norvig]] indicate that earning trust can involve [[verification and validation]], certification, transparency, and [[Explainable artificial intelligence|explainability]].<ref name="aima42">{{Cite book |last1=Russell |first1=Stuart J. |url=https://www.pearson.com/us/higher-education/program/Russell-Artificial-Intelligence-A-Modern-Approach-4th-Edition/PGM1263338.html |title=Artificial intelligence: A modern approach |last2=Norvig |first2=Peter |publisher=Pearson |year=2021 |isbn=9780134610993 |edition=4th |access-date=September 12, 2022|chapter=28.3.4 Trust and transparency}}</ref>
